cards.front: A continuous amino-acid stretch that carries sorting information is a {{c1::signal sequence}}.
cards.back: It acts like an address for the protein.
cards.quote: A signal sequence is a continuous stretch of amino acids that carries sorting information, like a zip code on a parcel.
cards.section: The address, and how to test it

cards.front: Where does a eukaryotic protein with no sorting signal remain by default?
cards.back: In the cytosol.
cards.quote: A protein with no signal stays in the cytosol by default, which gives the field its two tests.
cards.section: The address, and how to test it

cards.front: How do gain-of-function and deletion tests distinguish signal sufficiency from necessity?
cards.back: A transferred signal that redirects a cytosolic protein is sufficient; deletion that prevents sorting shows it is necessary.
cards.quote: If moving a stretch onto a protein that normally stays in the cytosol moves that protein, the stretch is sufficient to sort it.
cards.section: The address, and how to test it

cards.front: Signal reading while a chain grows is {{c1::cotranslational}}; reading after release is post-translational.
cards.back: The terms describe when targeting information is read relative to translation.
cards.quote: reading "as the chain grows" is cotranslational, and reading "after release" is post-translational.

cards.front: A typical ER signal is a {{c1::hydrophobic stretch near the amino terminus}}.
cards.back: Its early position permits recognition while translation continues.
cards.quote: The amino terminus leaves the ribosome first (translation), and the ER signal is a hydrophobic stretch, usually near the amino terminus.
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: How does SRP begin cotranslational targeting of a secretory protein to the ER?
cards.back: SRP recognizes the emerging ER signal and temporarily arrests or slows chain growth.
cards.quote: in a translation extract made from wheat germ, SRP stopped the growth of preprolactin chains at about 70 residues
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: What did release of the SRP-induced preprolactin translation stop after adding ER vesicles show?
cards.back: It linked the stop to ER targeting: membrane addition allowed the arrested targeting intermediate to resume elongation.
cards.quote: Adding ER vesicles released the stop. (In other extracts SRP only slows chain growth for a while; Going deeper.)
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: High-salt washing makes ER vesicles unable to bind prolactin-making ribosomes. Purified SRP restores binding. What does this result support?
cards.back: SRP is required for productive docking of the signal-bearing ribosome at the ER membrane.
cards.quote: washing dog-pancreas ER vesicles in high salt removed their ability to bind ribosomes making prolactin, and purified SRP restored it
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: How do the GTPases of SRP and the SRP receptor coordinate handover to Sec61?
cards.back: Their facing GTP sites promote reciprocal GTP hydrolysis; this drives complex disassembly after handover to the channel.
cards.quote: the GTP sites face each other, so each helps the other hydrolyse GTP and the complex comes apart.
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: ER signal peptidase acts on the {{c1::lumenal side}} of the membrane.
cards.back: Many membrane-protein signals instead remain uncleaved as anchors.
cards.quote: Signal peptidase works on the lumenal side of the membrane. Many membrane proteins keep an uncleaved signal that stays in the membrane as an anchor.
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: A 60-residue secretory protein has an ER signal at residues 1–20, and about 40 residues remain hidden in the ribosome. At what chain length has the whole signal emerged?
cards.back: 20 + 40 = 60 residues. The signal clears only as synthesis finishes, leaving SRP almost no time to bind.
cards.quote: Only when the chain is about 60 residues long (20 + 40), that is, when it is finished.
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: A secreted protein's hydrophobic ER signal is moved to its carboxyl terminus. Ignoring tail-anchor insertion, what happens and why?
cards.back: It is made in the cytosol and largely remains there. The signal emerges only upon release, too late for SRP-mediated cotranslational targeting.
cards.quote: A signal at the carboxyl end is the extreme case: it leaves the ribosome only as the chain is released
cards.section: Into the ER while being made

cards.front: Sealed vesicles formed from disrupted ER membrane are called {{c1::microsomes}}.
cards.back: They support cell-free tests of ER translocation.
cards.quote: Some reactions include microsomes, sealed vesicles formed from ER membrane when cells are broken up.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: Why does survival after external protease indicate that a translated protein entered sealed microsomes?
cards.back: Protease cannot cross an intact membrane, so the vesicle lumen shields imported chains while exposed chains are digested.
cards.quote: Assume the protease cannot cross an intact membrane and that the bands are proportional to the amount of protein.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: With microsomes present during translation, an unprocessed 26-kDa precursor band vanishes after protease. Was that precursor inside the vesicles, and why?
cards.back: No. Its complete digestion shows it was exposed outside; failure to enter also explains why its signal remained uncleaved.
cards.quote: After protease no 26 kDa band survives, so every unprocessed chain was outside and was digested.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: Of 60 units of processed secretory protein, 57 survive protease. What percentage of processed chains were protected inside sealed microsomes?
cards.back: 57 / 60 × 100% = 95%. Nearly all processed chains were protected.
cards.quote: protected fraction = 57 / 60 = 0.95, or 95 percent So nearly all processed chains are inside sealed vesicles.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: Why does loss of a protease-protected band after detergent confirm membrane translocation?
cards.back: Detergent dissolves the protective vesicle membrane, exposing the chain; therefore protection was not an intrinsic resistance to protease.
cards.quote: The protein is not resistant to protease on its own; the membrane protected it.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: Microsomes added after translation yield neither signal cleavage nor protease protection. What does this show in this assay?
cards.back: ER translocation requires ongoing translation; adding the membrane after chain release is too late.
cards.quote: In lane 3 there is no processing and no protection. In this assay, translocation needs ongoing translation.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: Signal cleavage changes a protein from 26 kDa to 23 kDa. Using 110 Da per residue, about how many residues were removed?
cards.quote: With an average residue mass of about 110 Da: residues removed ≈ 3,000 Da / 110 Da per residue ≈ 27 residues
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a protection gel

cards.front: A mitochondrial matrix protein commonly carries an amino-terminal presequence read by {{c1::TOM receptors}} at the outer membrane.
cards.back: The presequence is an amphipathic helix.
cards.quote: They work away from the ribosome's exit: TOM on the mitochondrial outer membrane, TOC on the chloroplast outer envelope, and PEX5 in the cytosol.

cards.front: A chloroplast precursor crosses the outer envelope through TOC and the inner envelope through {{c1::TIC}}.
cards.back: Its amino-terminal transit peptide is usually removed in the stroma.
cards.quote: Chloroplasts follow the mitochondrial pattern, through TOC in the outer envelope and TIC in the inner.

cards.front: The carboxyl-terminal PTS1 signal recognized by PEX5 can be the tripeptide {{c1::SKL}}.
cards.back: PTS1 is usually not cleaved after peroxisomal import.
cards.quote: A protein ends in SKL and goes to peroxisomes.

cards.front: How does the usual timing of ER targeting differ from targeting to mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes?
cards.back: ER signals are usually read during synthesis; the other three organelles usually read their cargo after chain release.
cards.quote: Their cargo is usually read after release. The reader's place does not settle the timing alone; the exceptions are in Going deeper.

cards.front: What energy inputs drive mitochondrial matrix import, and what does each do?
cards.back: Inner-membrane potential acts on the presequence; ATP powers matrix Hsp70.
cards.quote: Then the presequence is pulled through the TIM23 complex, is often cut off in the matrix

cards.front: What energy source powers chloroplast import on the stromal side?
cards.back: ATP, although which ATP-driven motor does most of the work remains debated.
cards.quote: Which ATP-driven motor pulls hardest is still debated (Going deeper).

cards.front: Which cytosolic receptor reads the amino-terminal peroxisomal signal PTS2?
cards.back: PEX7.
cards.quote: PEX7 reads PTS2 cargo as PEX5 reads PTS1.

cards.front: How does cargo folding during peroxisomal import differ from mitochondrial and chloroplast import?
cards.back: Peroxisomes can import folded cargo, even oligomers; mitochondrial cargo must unfold at least partly, and chloroplast cargo crosses largely unfolded.
cards.quote: The evidence that cargo can stay folded came in 1995: Walton, Hill and Subramani found that mammalian peroxisomes imported proteins held folded

cards.front: Methotrexate prevents import of a mitochondrial-presequence–DHFR fusion, but an authentic precursor still imports. What does the control establish?
cards.back: The mitochondria and membrane potential still work. The block is specific to holding the DHFR passenger folded, so import requires partial unfolding.
cards.quote: the authentic precursor still entered the same mitochondria, so the organelles and their membrane potential were working and the block was in the passenger.

cards.front: A mitochondrial matrix precursor is incubated with isolated mitochondria, with or without an uncoupler, then protease is added. What happens and why?
cards.back: Only without uncoupler does a protected, smaller product appear. Membrane potential permits import and processing; the membranes then protect the chain.
cards.quote: With the uncoupler, complete TIM23-mediated import and processing are blocked; the precursor may bind or partly engage the machinery

cards.front: Peroxisomes import cross-linked proteins and signal-coated gold particles. What does this evidence show?
cards.back: Peroxisomal cargo can remain folded, and even large signal-bearing assemblies can enter.
cards.quote: mammalian peroxisomes imported proteins held folded by disulfide bonds or chemical cross-links, and even gold particles coated with signal-bearing protein.

cards.front: GFP is fused after the terminal SKL of a peroxisomal protein. Where does the fusion most likely go, and why?
cards.back: It most likely stays in the cytosol. SKL is no longer at the free carboxyl end, so PEX5 should not recognize it.
cards.quote: PEX5 holds the free carboxyl end of a PTS1 deep in its groove

cards.front: How do the DHFR-presequence fusion and luciferase-tail deletion together establish the signal-sequence model?
cards.back: The presequence redirects a foreign passenger, showing sufficiency; tail deletion prevents peroxisomal targeting, showing necessity. The rule is that gain and loss tests establish complementary causal roles.
cards.quote: Each classic result is one of the two tests. Sufficient: the first 53 residues of a yeast mitochondrial precursor carried mouse DHFR into the matrix

cards.front: A sorting sequence redirects a passenger when terminal but fails after being moved inside the chain. What principle explains the change?
cards.back: Position is part of signal function: recognition can require emergence at the right time or accessibility at a free terminus.
cards.quote: position matters: a signal that works at one end may fail at the other or inside the chain.

cards.front: Can two recognizable targeting signals alone determine which organelle receives a protein?
cards.back: No. Their competition is empirical; signal order can suggest a hypothesis but does not settle the outcome.
cards.quote: When a protein carries two signals, the outcome is empirical.

cards.front: Protein Y has an amino-terminal amphipathic helix and terminal SKL. Design a localization test that separates the roles of both signals.
cards.back: Compare full-length, helix-deleted, SKL-deleted, and double-deleted Y constructs with GFP inserted just after the helix against mitochondrial and peroxisomal markers. This keeps SKL free and tests each signal alone and together.
cards.quote: Build four GFP fusions: full-length Y, Y without the helix, Y without SKL, and Y without both.

cards.front: How would protease and an uncoupler distinguish mitochondrial import of Protein Y from surface sticking?
cards.back: Import Y into isolated mitochondria ± uncoupler, then add protease. Protected, processed Y only with membrane potential indicates import. The rules are protease protection, processing, and energy dependence.
cards.quote: Protected, processed Y that disappears with the uncoupler means import, not sticking to the surface.

cards.front: A protein is protease-protected in intact mitochondria. How can swelling help test whether it reached the matrix?
cards.back: Open the outer membrane by swelling and repeat protease treatment. Persistence of protection supports an inner-membrane-enclosed location. The rule is to remove one barrier at a time.
cards.quote: To show it reached the matrix, open the outer membrane by swelling and repeat the protease test.

cards.front: After rapid SRP depletion in budding yeast, many cleavable-signal proteins retain ER-proximal ribosomes, whereas transmembrane proteins lose them. What model fits both observations?
cards.back: In budding yeast, some cleavable-signal proteins use SRP-independent targeting, while transmembrane proteins generally require SRP. The perturbation reveals parallel routes with different cargo dependence.
cards.quote: rapid SRP depletion in 2018 left many proteins with cleavable signals still targeted while being made

cards.front: A protein's only hydrophobic segment is at its extreme carboxyl end. Why can it still enter the ER membrane after SRP misses it?
cards.back: It can use the post-translational GET/TRC40 tail-anchor route because the terminal segment emerges only when translation ends.
cards.quote: Tail-anchored proteins, whose only hydrophobic segment is at the very end, are inserted after translation by other machinery

cards.front: Three soluble proteins carry, respectively, an amino-terminal hydrophobic stretch, an amino-terminal amphipathic helix, or terminal SKL. Predict their main destinations and targeting times.
cards.back: ER during synthesis; mitochondrial matrix usually after release; peroxisomal matrix after release. The rules are signal identity and its usual reader timing, while exceptions remain possible.
cards.quote: The reader's place does not settle the timing alone; the exceptions are in Going deeper.
